title: Inside South Korea's robot park, the humanoid future still has some way to go
key_facts: Galaxy Robot Park in Seoul opened this summer, run by South Korean company Galaxy Corporation.
Ten Unitree humanoid robots perform a 50-minute dance and martial arts show.
Slow routines look jerky and the robots' moves are far more limited than those of human taekwondo fighters who join the show.
A humanoid that seems to chat with visitors is actually driven by a handler with a controller behind his back; boxing and football robots are also remote-controlled.
A bartender robot made of two arms on a sphere, with no legs or face, is among the most practical machines in the park.
Investors bet on a ChatGPT-style breakthrough in humanoids, but robots lack an internet-scale supply of training data.
quote_evidence: A visit to Galaxy Robot Park in Seoul, however, reveals a considerable gap between what humanoid robots appear capable of doing and how independently they can actually operate, the New York Times reported.
A humanoid that appears to interact with visitors is actually being operated by a nearby handler holding a controller behind his back.
A robotic bartender consists of two mechanical arms mounted on a large sphere.
why_it_matters_hint: Choreographed robot shows can overstate how independent humanoid robots really are.
event_date: Park opened summer 2026; NYT report relayed 6 Oct 2026
notes: Moneycontrol rewrites a New York Times report; NYT original not read. Funny detail (handler hiding a controller) is confirmed in the text.
